why: Ranking on test macro F1 (mean ± std, 3 seeds): 1D-CNN 93.32 ± 0.51 > BiLSTM 90.90 ± 1.11 > Transformer 87.93 ± 1.65. The CNN gap over the BiLSTM (about 2.4 points) is larger than either model's seed spread; the BiLSTM vs Transformer gap (about 3 points) is too.

The CNN is also the most stable across seeds (smallest std) and the cheapest: 127,494 parameters and 0.29 ms per window on CPU at batch 1, versus 1.70 ms (BiLSTM, about 6x slower) and 1.28 ms (Transformer).

The Transformer has the fewest parameters (101,574) but is the slowest when windows are batched (1.62 ms per window at batch 256 vs 0.66 BiLSTM and 0.16 CNN), because self-attention over 128 timesteps scales with the square of the sequence length. Explain this trade-off.

Where the models differ is on the moving activities, not the postures: per-class F1 for Walking is 0.994 (CNN), 0.959 (BiLSTM), 0.876 (Transformer). Moving-to-moving confusions per seed: CNN about 15, BiLSTM about 46, Transformer about 155.

Possible explanation to argue in your own words: walking-type signals are short repeated motion patterns; convolution has a built-in bias for local, shift-invariant patterns, while the Transformer must learn locality from only 5,905 training windows. Link to [5] (no family wins everywhere) and to the small-data risk in IV-C.
All three models score 0.99 to 1.00 macro F1 on validation but 0.88 to 0.93 on test. The 4 validation subjects are much easier than the 9 test subjects, so validation scores cannot rank the models.

Because validation saturates, early stopping picked very early checkpoints in most runs (best epoch 2 to 7 in 7 of 9 runs). The Transformer in particular stopped at 10 to 15 epochs. This is a real limitation: the Transformer may be under-trained under this shared budget. Say so, do not hide it.

Compared with the literature on UCI HAR: our CNN (93.15% mean accuracy) is below Ronao and Cho's 94.79% [2] and our BiLSTM (90.7% accuracy) is below Zhao et al.'s 93.57% [6]; we do no tuning, use fewer training subjects (4 held out), and report the mean over seeds rather than a best run.

Interim to final change: the interim single run (seed 42) gave CNN 92.98% and BiLSTM 91.14%. The final seed-42 runs give 92.91% and 92.09% most likely because the final runs used 1 CPU thread each (re-running the interim setup with default threads reproduced the interim CNN numbers exactly). This is exactly why we now report mean ± std over 3 seeds.
errors: Sitting vs Standing is the main failure for every model: per seed, about 168 (CNN), 194 (BiLSTM) and 189 (Transformer) test windows are confused between these two. That is 83%, 71% and 53% of each model's errors.

Because all three families make about the same number of Sitting/Standing errors, the limit is likely in the data, not the architecture: both postures give near-flat signals that differ mainly in how gravity falls on the phone at the waist. Compare with the 88% Sitting recall of the SVM in [1].
Laying is almost never wrong for the CNN and Transformer (0 errors per seed), but the BiLSTM misclassifies about 18 Laying windows per seed, mostly as Upstairs.
The Transformer's second-largest error source is Walking predicted as Downstairs (48 to 93 windows per seed) and, in seed 42, Upstairs predicted as Walking (58 windows).

Errors are concentrated in a few people. Mean test accuracy for subject 10: CNN 74.7%, BiLSTM 65.3%, Transformer 61.7%; subject 9: 83.0%, 78.2%, 66.0%. Subjects 12, 13, 18, 20 and 24 are at 90% to 99% for all models. The same two subjects are hardest for all three families, which points to subject-specific behaviour (for example how they sit or stand), not a model bug.

conclusion: Best model on every metric we measured: 1D-CNN (highest macro F1, lowest variance, fastest, mid-size).
BiLSTM second on accuracy, slowest at batch 1 because it processes 128 steps one after another.
Transformer last on accuracy under our shared budget; fewest parameters but most expensive when batched.
Shared limit: Sitting vs Standing, and two hard test subjects (9, 10).
